Reference: Oberfield (2018)

Model Setting

The paper asks why producers differ so much in size and in their engagement in input-output linkages, and what this heterogeneity implies for aggregate productivity. It develops a theory in which the input-output architecture of the economy, that is, who buys inputs from whom, forms endogenously. Each entrepreneur produces with labor and exactly one intermediate input, and the key decision is which other entrepreneur's good to use. A technique is a buyer-supplier pair with a random match-specific productivity, techniques arrive by a Poisson process, and the set of techniques forms a random weighted directed graph of potential suppliers and potential customers. Each entrepreneur selects the most cost-effective technique, and these selections jointly determine the supply chains used, each producer's size and aggregate productivity. Sales to the household are monopolistically competitive, while sales of intermediates are governed by bilateral contracts that must be stable against deviations by coalitions.

There are four sets of results. First, every countably-stable equilibrium is efficient and the allocation is essentially unique; the cross-sectional distribution of efficiencies solves a fixed point problem, and when match-specific productivities have a power-law tail with exponent ζ\zetaζ this distribution is Frechet and aggregate output has a closed form. Second, star suppliers emerge endogenously: the distribution of customers has a power-law tail with exponent 1/α1/\alpha1/α, where α\alphaα is the elasticity of output with respect to the intermediate input, and it does not depend on ζ\zetaζ, so large differences in size arise even when differences in marginal cost are arbitrarily small. The size distribution has a threshold property: its right tail has exponent min⁡{1/α,ζ/(ε−1)}\min\{1/\alpha,\zeta/(\varepsilon-1)\}min{1/α,ζ/(ε−1)}. Third, among matches used in equilibrium the efficiencies of buyers and suppliers are uncorrelated but their employment is positively correlated. Fourth, the aggregate cost share of intermediates exceeds α\alphaα when suppliers have bargaining power, so it is not a sufficient statistic for the input-output multiplier, and a higher α\alphaα raises aggregate productivity both through the usual multiplier and by routing supply chains through higher-productivity techniques.

Stability and Equilibrium

A coalition is a set of entrepreneurs. A deviation by a coalition consists of dropping any contracts that involve at least one of its members and altering the terms of any contract whose buyer and supplier are both members. A dominating deviation leaves every member weakly better off and at least one strictly better off. An arrangement is NNN-stable if no coalition of cardinality NNN or smaller has a dominating deviation. The paper focuses on countably-stable arrangements, for which no countable coalition has a dominating deviation, and compares them with pairwise stable ones (N=2N=2N=2). An NNN-stable equilibrium is an arrangement, entrepreneurs' choices and a wage such that the household maximizes utility, each entrepreneur maximizes her payoff given the arrangement, labor and final goods markets clear, no coalition of the specified size has a dominating deviation, and the allocation is feasible.

Let λj\lambda_jλj​ be the marginal cost of entrepreneur jjj, the multiplier on her technological constraint. She charges the household the usual markup, pj=εε−1λjp_j=\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}\lambda_jpj​=ε−1ε​λj​, and hires labor so that wl(ϕ)=(1−α)λjy(ϕ)wl(\phi)=(1-\alpha)\lambda_jy(\phi)wl(ϕ)=(1−α)λj​y(ϕ). Define the efficiency of jjj as the inverse of her marginal cost in units of labor, qj≡w/λjq_j\equiv w/\lambda_jqj​≡w/λj​. Proposition 1 has three parts. First, in any pairwise-stable equilibrium:

cj=qjεQ1−εL,C=QL,Q≡(∫01qjε−1dj)1ε−1(7)c_j=q_j^\varepsilon Q^{1-\varepsilon}L,\qquad C=QL,\qquad Q\equiv\left(\int_0^1q_j^{\varepsilon-1}dj\right)^{\frac{1}{\varepsilon-1}} \tag{7}cj​=qjε​Q1−εL,C=QL,Q≡(∫01​qjε−1​dj)ε−11​(7)

qj=max⁡ϕ∈Ujz(ϕ)qs(ϕ)α(8)q_j=\max_{\phi\in U_j}z(\phi)q_{s(\phi)}^\alpha \tag{8}qj​=ϕ∈Uj​max​z(ϕ)qs(ϕ)α​(8)

with qj=0q_j=0qj​=0 if UjU_jUj​ is empty, together with the bound qj≤sup⁡ω∈Ωj∏n=0∞[zn(ω)]αnq_j\leq\sup_{\omega\in\Omega_j}\prod_{n=0}^\infty[z^n(\omega)]^{\alpha^n}qj​≤supω∈Ωj​​∏n=0∞​[zn(ω)]αn. Second, in any countably-stable equilibrium the efficiency of jjj equals that of her best supply chain:

qj=sup⁡ω∈Ωj∏n=0∞[zn(ω)]αn(9)q_j=\sup_{\omega\in\Omega_j}\prod_{n=0}^\infty\left[z^n(\omega)\right]^{\alpha^n} \tag{9}qj​=ω∈Ωj​sup​n=0∏∞​[zn(ω)]αn(9)

with qj=0q_j=0qj​=0 if Ωj\Omega_jΩj​ is empty. Third, every countably-stable equilibrium is efficient, and if HHH is atomless then with probability 1 the allocation consistent with countable stability is essentially unique.

The intuition of the proof is as follows. Pairwise stability implies that for every technique:

λb(ϕ)≤1z(ϕ)λs(ϕ)αw1−α(10)\lambda_{b(\phi)}\leq\frac{1}{z(\phi)}\lambda_{s(\phi)}^\alpha w^{1-\alpha} \tag{10}λb(ϕ)​≤z(ϕ)1​λs(ϕ)α​w1−α(10)

with equality if x(ϕ)>0x(\phi)>0x(ϕ)>0. A buyer and supplier who maximize their bilateral gains from trade choose a quantity at which the buyer's shadow value of the input equals the supplier's marginal cost, so no supply chain suffers from double marginalization; collecting this condition over UjU_jUj​ gives the recursion, and each entrepreneur's marginal cost in units of labor equals the labor used across all stages of her supply chains per unit of her good, which gives C=QLC=QLC=QL. The upper bound follows from iterating the recursion along a chain and imposing chain feasibility. Pairwise stability alone is weak: there is always a pairwise stable equilibrium in which no entrepreneur produces. If instead some jjj had efficiency below that of one of her chains, the countable coalition formed by the entrepreneurs along that chain would have a dominating deviation in which each produces slightly more, raising the profit of jjj by enough to compensate all of them. Efficiency follows from the planner's problem for a single chain: a planner who allocates lll units of labor across the stages of chain ω\omegaω solves:

and obtains the indirect production function c(ω)=∏n=0∞[zn(ω)]αnlc(\omega)=\prod_{n=0}^\infty[z^n(\omega)]^{\alpha^n}lc(ω)=∏n=0∞​[zn(ω)]αnl, so each entrepreneur's equilibrium marginal cost equals the planner's shadow cost of her good. Markups on sales to the household do not distort the allocation because labor is supplied inelastically and the demand elasticity is common. The allocation fails to be unique only if an entrepreneur has two techniques that deliver exactly the same efficiency, which has probability zero.

Countable stability pins down quantities but not payments. In any countably-stable equilibrium the profit of jjj can be written as:

The surplus generated by technique ϕ\phiϕ is its contribution to all entrepreneurs' profit from sales to the household:

An entrepreneur is acyclic if there is at most one (undirected) path of techniques linking her to any other entrepreneur; J∗J^*J∗ is the set of acyclic entrepreneurs, which has measure 1 with probability 1, and Φ∗\Phi^*Φ∗ is the set of techniques whose buyer and supplier are acyclic. Proposition 2 states that in any countably-stable equilibrium τ(ϕ)∈[0,S(ϕ)]\tau(\phi)\in[0,\mathcal{S}(\phi)]τ(ϕ)∈[0,S(ϕ)] for each ϕ∈Φ∗\phi\in\Phi^*ϕ∈Φ∗, and that for any β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1]β∈[0,1] there exists a countably-stable equilibrium in which τ(ϕ)=βS(ϕ)\tau(\phi)=\beta\mathcal{S}(\phi)τ(ϕ)=βS(ϕ) for all ϕ∈Φ∗\phi\in\Phi^*ϕ∈Φ∗ and τ(ϕ)=0\tau(\phi)=0τ(ϕ)=0 for all ϕ∉Φ∗\phi\notin\Phi^*ϕ∈/Φ∗. If τ(ϕ)<0\tau(\phi)<0τ(ϕ)<0 the supplier would drop the contract and her whole chain would shrink production efficiently, leaving her marginal cost unchanged; if τ(ϕ)>S(ϕ)\tau(\phi)>\mathcal{S}(\phi)τ(ϕ)>S(ϕ) the buyer would drop the contract and switch to her next best technique, whose chain would expand efficiently. The parameter β\betaβ is the bargaining power of suppliers, analogous to generalized Nash bargaining except that the surplus a pair splits depends on how the buyer splits surplus with her own buyers. Bargaining power affects payments, and hence observed transactions, but not the allocation.

and a mixture of Poisson distributions inherits the right tail of the mixing distribution, here a power law in the mean number of customers uuu. At the ϱ\varrhoϱ-th quantile of the efficiency distribution the mean number of customers is log⁡[1/ϱ]−αΓ(1−α)\frac{\log[1/\varrho]^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}Γ(1−α)log[1/ϱ]−α​, which depends only on α\alphaα and is more steeply increasing in ϱ\varrhoϱ when α\alphaα is higher (a single crossing property).

The economics is selection. The efficiency delivered by a technique is z(ϕ)qs(ϕ)αz(\phi)q_{s(\phi)}^\alphaz(ϕ)qs(ϕ)α​, so α\alphaα is the elasticity of that efficiency with respect to the supplier's efficiency. When α\alphaα is low, the supplier's cost matters little relative to the match-specific productivity; when α\alphaα is high, low-cost entrepreneurs are selected more systematically by their potential customers and become star suppliers. Potential customers are Poisson, with a thin tail, but actual customers have a power-law tail; the mean number of actual customers is 1 and their variance exceeds 1. The mechanism complements the preferential attachment model of Barabasi and Albert (1999). The distribution does not depend on ζ\zetaζ because ζ\zetaζ plays two offsetting roles: a smaller ζ\zetaζ raises the variation in match-specific draws, which compresses the customer distribution, and it endogenously raises the variation in suppliers' costs, which spreads it. Nor does it depend on mmm: more techniques give each entrepreneur more potential customers but give each of those customers more alternatives. The independence from the dispersion of marginal cost does not rely on Assumption 2. In a γ\gammaγ-economy in which each zzz is replaced by z^≡zγ\hat{z}\equiv z^\gammaz^≡zγ, the efficiency delivered by chain ω\omegaω is:

∏n=0∞[z^n(ω)]αn=(∏n=0∞[zn(ω)]αn)γ(21)\prod_{n=0}^\infty\left[\hat{z}^n(\omega)\right]^{\alpha^n}=\left(\prod_{n=0}^\infty\left[z^n(\omega)\right]^{\alpha^n}\right)^\gamma \tag{21}n=0∏∞​[z^n(ω)]αn=(n=0∏∞​[zn(ω)]αn)γ(21)

so q^j=qjγ\hat{q}_j=q_j^\gammaq^​j​=qjγ​: the dispersion of log efficiencies is proportional to γ\gammaγ, but the ranking of supply chains, and hence the equilibrium network, is independent of γ\gammaγ.

and a Tauberian theorem (valid for non-integer ρ\rhoρ) relates the behavior of the transform at zero to the right tail. The shape of the distribution depends only on α\alphaα and ε−1ζ\frac{\varepsilon-1}{\zeta}ζε−1​. Labor used to make intermediates for others has a Pareto tail with exponent 1/α1/\alpha1/α, labor used to make consumption has a Pareto tail with exponent ζ/(ε−1)\zeta/(\varepsilon-1)ζ/(ε−1), and the thicker tail dominates. Average employment among entrepreneurs with efficiency qqq is (1−α)(q/Q)ε−1L+αmθqαζL(1-\alpha)(q/Q)^{\varepsilon-1}L+\alpha\frac{m}{\theta}q^{\alpha\zeta}L(1−α)(q/Q)ε−1L+αθm​qαζL. When α\alphaα is small the model resembles canonical models in which the right tail reflects sales to the household and depends on the dispersion of marginal cost. When α>ε−1ζ\alpha>\frac{\varepsilon-1}{\zeta}α>ζε−1​ the tail is dominated by star suppliers and has exponent 1/α1/\alpha1/α, whatever the dispersion of efficiency. The second result says that size varies greatly even among entrepreneurs with the same efficiency, who have identical sales to the household and a thin-tailed Poisson number of customers. The source is the granularity of customers: a customer may itself be a star supplier, so the conditional distribution inherits the tail of the overall distribution, scaled by the expected number of customers and by the factor α\alphaα that converts a customer's labor into the supplier's labor. In the language of Acemoglu, Carvalho, Ozdaglar and Tahbaz-Salehi (2012), the first result reflects first-order and the second reflects second-order interconnections.

Proposition 6 states that under Assumption 2, among techniques used in equilibrium, Cov(log⁡qb(ϕ),log⁡qs(ϕ))=0\text{Cov}(\log q_{b(\phi)},\log q_{s(\phi)})=0Cov(logqb(ϕ)​,logqs(ϕ)​)=0; Cov(nb(ϕ),ns(ϕ))=0\text{Cov}(n_{b(\phi)},n_{s(\phi)})=0Cov(nb(ϕ)​,ns(ϕ)​)=0, where njn_jnj​ is the number of customers of jjj; and Cov(lb(ϕ),ls(ϕ))>0\text{Cov}(l_{b(\phi)},l_{s(\phi)})>0Cov(lb(ϕ)​,ls(ϕ)​)>0. For the first result, a supplier with efficiency qsq_sqs​ is selected through a downstream technique with productivity zzz with probability F~(zqsα)\tilde{F}(zq_s^\alpha)F~(zqsα​), so the distribution of the efficiency qbq_bqb​ of her actual customers is:

which is independent of qsq_sqs​. Selection drives the result: a technique with a low-efficiency supplier is chosen only if its match-specific productivity is unusually high, while a technique with a high-efficiency supplier may be chosen even with a poor match, so that among used techniques lower-efficiency suppliers have better matches and the two efficiencies are uncorrelated (exactly zero only under Assumption 2). The second result follows because the rate at which an entrepreneur is selected as a supplier depends only on her efficiency. For the third, the supplier needs αlb\alpha l_bαlb​ units of labor to make the inputs of a buyer who uses lbl_blb​, and the other components of her labor are uncorrelated with lbl_blb​, so the covariance equals αVar(l)>0\alpha\text{Var}(l)>0αVar(l)>0. Whether matching is assortative thus depends on the attribute studied.

Aggregate Output

Combining C=QLC=QLC=QL with the Frechet distribution and the expression for θ\thetaθ:

Q=θ1/ζΓ(1−ε−1ζ)1ε−1,C=[Γ(1−ε−1ζ)ζε−1Γ(1−α)11−αm11−α]1ζL(29)Q=\theta^{1/\zeta}\Gamma\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon-1}{\zeta}\right)^{\frac{1}{\varepsilon-1}},\qquad C=\left[\Gamma\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon-1}{\zeta}\right)^{\frac{\zeta}{\varepsilon-1}}\Gamma(1-\alpha)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}m^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}\right]^{\frac{1}{\zeta}}L \tag{29}Q=θ1/ζΓ(1−ζε−1​)ε−11​,C=[Γ(1−ζε−1​)ε−1ζ​Γ(1−α)1−α1​m1−α1​]ζ1​L(29)

Output increases with the measure of techniques mmm, as in Kortum (1997), whose model is nested when α=0\alpha=0α=0. The exponent 1ζ\frac{1}{\zeta}ζ1​ scales the productivity of every technique, and the term Γ(1−ε−1ζ)ζε−1\Gamma\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon-1}{\zeta}\right)^{\frac{\zeta}{\varepsilon-1}}Γ(1−ζε−1​)ε−1ζ​ reflects the household's substitution toward cheaper goods. The parameter α\alphaα has two roles. The exponent 11−α\frac{1}{1-\alpha}1−α1​ is the standard input-output multiplier of roundabout production, with the difference that α\alphaα is smaller than the cost share when β>0\beta>0β>0. The term Γ(1−α)\Gamma(1-\alpha)Γ(1−α) is new: it captures the composition of suppliers. When α\alphaα is closer to 1 the lowest-cost producers are more likely to become star suppliers and supply chains are more likely to be routed through higher-productivity techniques, which are then used more intensively. As a numerical illustration, raising α\alphaα from 0.55 to 0.65 increases the standard multiplier 11−α\frac{1}{1-\alpha}1−α1​ from 2.2 to 2.9, increases Γ(1−α)\Gamma(1-\alpha)Γ(1−α) by a factor of 1.3 and increases Γ(1−α)11−α\Gamma(1-\alpha)^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}Γ(1−α)1−α1​ by a factor of 3.2.

Identification and Quantitative Illustration

The paper does not estimate the model; it suggests identification strategies and offers illustrations. Because the cost share does not reveal α\alphaα, the multiplier must be measured directly: an iceberg cost δ>1\delta>1δ>1 on all shipments is isomorphic to dividing every match-specific productivity by δ\deltaδ, which divides the efficiency of every supply chain by δ11−α\delta^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}δ1−α1​, so dln⁡Qdln⁡δ=−11−α\frac{d\ln Q}{d\ln\delta}=-\frac{1}{1-\alpha}dlnδdlnQ​=−1−α1​. The parameter ζ\zetaζ plays the role of the trade elasticity in Eaton and Kortum (2002). If entrepreneurs are randomly divided into groups J1,…,JKJ_1,\ldots,J_KJ1​,…,JK​ of sizes μ1,…,μK\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_Kμ1​,…,μK​ and the sales of group kkk are taxed at the proportional rate δk−1\delta_k-1δk​−1, relative intermediate purchases from two groups are:

∫j∈Jk∑ϕ∈DjT(ϕ)∫j∈Jk′∑ϕ∈DjT(ϕ)=μkδk−ζμk′δk′−ζ(30)\frac{\int_{j\in J_k}\sum_{\phi\in D_j}T(\phi)}{\int_{j\in J_{k'}}\sum_{\phi\in D_j}T(\phi)}=\frac{\mu_k\delta_k^{-\zeta}}{\mu_{k'}\delta_{k'}^{-\zeta}} \tag{30}∫j∈Jk′​​∑ϕ∈Dj​​T(ϕ)∫j∈Jk​​∑ϕ∈Dj​​T(ϕ)​=μk′​δk′−ζ​μk​δk−ζ​​(30)

so the elasticity of relative purchases with respect to δk/δk′\delta_k/\delta_{k'}δk​/δk′​ is −ζ-\zeta−ζ. The elasticity ε\varepsilonε is identified from household substitution across goods, and β\betaβ from the aggregate cost share given α\alphaα and ζ\zetaζ.

  • Customer distribution: under Assumption 2 the conditional means and the unconditional distribution of customers depend only on α\alphaα. The paper plots mean customers by efficiency quantile for α=0.25\alpha=0.25α=0.25 and 0.500.500.50 (the curves cross once, near the 0.8 quantile) and the mass of entrepreneurs with nnn customers for α=0.25\alpha=0.25α=0.25, 0.500.500.50 and 0.750.750.75, whose tail is visibly thicker for higher α\alphaα. The covariance between log⁡q\log qlogq and the number of customers divided by the standard deviation of log⁡q\log qlogq equals 6π∫01x−α−11−xdx\frac{\sqrt{6}}{\pi}\int_0^1\frac{x^{-\alpha}-1}{1-x}dxπ6​​∫01​1−xx−α−1​dx, which is increasing in α\alphaα.

  • Simulated networks: with the set of techniques held fixed (M=15M=15M=15 and H(z)=1−z−2H(z)=1-z^{-2}H(z)=1−z−2 for z≥1z\geq1z≥1), raising α\alphaα visibly concentrates the techniques used in equilibrium on a few star suppliers.

  • Cross-industry evidence (supplement): among French industries, using the tail exponents of firm revenue estimated by Di Giovanni, Levchenko and Ranciere (2011), industries with higher intermediate input shares tend to have thicker tails. For US establishments and firms, using data extracts from Rossi-Hansberg and Wright (2007), the point estimates have the same sign but are not statistically distinguishable from zero.

  • Caveats: with β>0\beta>0β>0 intermediate shares differ from α\alphaα; real producers use many inputs with varying shares; the empirical counterpart of an entrepreneur (firm, establishment or product) is unclear; and an exponent of 1/α1/\alpha1/α exceeds the exponent close to 1 (Zipf's law) of the empirical firm size distribution.

  • Extensions: ex ante asymmetries across goods (industries or countries) can be accommodated without loss of tractability, and the model could be modified to study distortions that lead producers to use the wrong suppliers, or changes in sourcing during crises and supply chain disruptions.

This is the assumed preference of the representative household: a constant elasticity of substitution (Dixit-Stiglitz) aggregate over the unit mass of differentiated goods. The term cjc_jcj​ is the quantity of good jjj consumed, CCC is the consumption bundle (a real quantity, also the measure of aggregate output), and ε\varepsilonε is the elasticity of substitution between any two goods. The note needs ε>1\varepsilon>1ε>1 so that goods are substitutes and the markup εε−1\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}ε−1ε​ is finite.

The form buys three things. First, the household's demand for each good is isoelastic with the same elasticity ε\varepsilonε for every good, which gives equation (4). Second, because the elasticity is common, every entrepreneur charges the same proportional markup over marginal cost, so relative prices equal relative marginal costs and markups do not distort the allocation when labor is supplied inelastically. Third, the aggregate is homogeneous of degree one, so that aggregate output is a productivity index times labor, C=QLC=QLC=QL in equation (7), where QQQ is the same type of aggregate applied to efficiencies with exponent ε−1\varepsilon-1ε−1.

The form rules out variable markups and any love-of-variety effect from the number of goods, which is fixed at one. The elasticity enters later results only through ε−1\varepsilon-1ε−1: it governs how strongly the household shifts spending to low-cost producers, so the tail of sales to the household has exponent ζ/(ε−1)\zeta/(\varepsilon-1)ζ/(ε−1) in equation (22), and finiteness of output requires ζ>ε−1\zeta>\varepsilon-1ζ>ε−1 in equation (29). In the limit of a very large ε\varepsilonε the household buys almost only from the most efficient producers:

cjci=(pjpi)−ε\frac{c_j}{c_i}=\left(\frac{p_j}{p_i}\right)^{-\varepsilon}ci​cj​​=(pi​pj​​)−ε

This is the assumed production function of a single technique. The buyer b(ϕ)b(\phi)b(ϕ) makes yyy units of her own good from xxx units of the good of the supplier s(ϕ)s(\phi)s(ϕ) and lll units of labor; zzz is the match-specific productivity of the technique, a Hicks-neutral shifter, and α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1)α∈(0,1) is the elasticity of output with respect to the intermediate input. The technology has constant returns to scale in the pair of inputs.

The constant 1αα(1−α)1−α\frac{1}{\alpha^\alpha(1-\alpha)^{1-\alpha}}αα(1−α)1−α1​ is a normalization that makes the unit cost function free of constants. If the buyer values the input at λs\lambda_sλs​ per unit and labor at www, cost minimization gives the unit cost

min⁡x,l{λsx+wl}  s.t.  1αα(1−α)1−αzxαl1−α=1⟹unit cost=1zλsαw1−α\min_{x,l}\left\{\lambda_sx+wl\right\}\ \text{ s.t. }\ \frac{1}{\alpha^\alpha(1-\alpha)^{1-\alpha}}zx^\alpha l^{1-\alpha}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{unit cost}=\frac{1}{z}\lambda_s^\alpha w^{1-\alpha}x,lmin​{λs​x+wl}  s.t.  αα(1−α)1−α1​zxαl1−α=1⟹unit cost=z1​λsα​w1−α

which is the right-hand side of equation (10). Dividing www by both sides gives the recursion for efficiencies in equation (8): a technique delivers efficiency zqsαzq_s^\alphazqsα​.

The Cobb-Douglas form implies constant cost shares at shadow prices, α\alphaα for the input and 1−α1-\alpha1−α for labor, which the note uses repeatedly in the form wl(ϕ)1−α=λs(ϕ)x(ϕ)α=λb(ϕ)y(ϕ)\frac{wl(\phi)}{1-\alpha}=\frac{\lambda_{s(\phi)}x(\phi)}{\alpha}=\lambda_{b(\phi)}y(\phi)1−αwl(ϕ)​=αλs(ϕ)​x(ϕ)​=λb(ϕ)​y(ϕ). It also makes the efficiency of a supply chain a product of productivities with geometric weights, equation (9). What it rules out is the use of several inputs at once and any substitution between the input and labor that would change cost shares. The parameter α\alphaα is the key parameter of the paper: it is the elasticity of the buyer's efficiency with respect to the supplier's efficiency, and it determines the tail of the customer distribution in equation (19) and the input-output multiplier 11−α\frac{1}{1-\alpha}1−α1​ in equation (29).

This is the definition of the payoff of entrepreneur jjj for a given arrangement. Revenue has two parts: pjcjp_jc_jpj​cj​ from sales to the household, and the payments T(ϕ)T(\phi)T(ϕ) received on the downstream techniques ϕ∈Dj\phi\in D_jϕ∈Dj​, for which jjj is the supplier. Costs also have two parts for every upstream technique ϕ∈Uj\phi\in U_jϕ∈Uj​, for which jjj is the buyer: the payment T(ϕ)T(\phi)T(ϕ) to the supplier and the wage bill wl(ϕ)wl(\phi)wl(ϕ) of the labor used with that technique.

The important point is what is chosen and what is taken as given. The quantities x(ϕ)x(\phi)x(ϕ) and payments T(ϕ)T(\phi)T(ϕ) of all contracts are fixed by the arrangement, so inside this problem they are constants. The entrepreneur chooses only the price pjp_jpj​, the sales cjc_jcj​ to the household and the labor l(ϕ)l(\phi)l(ϕ) combined with each contracted input. The constraints are the demand curve in equation (4) and the technological constraint in equation (5). Since payments are lump sums from the point of view of this problem, they do not affect the marginal choices; this is why two-part contracts can avoid double marginalization.

Let λj\lambda_jλj​ be the multiplier on equation (5). The first-order conditions of the problem are the ones quoted in the note:

pj=εε−1λj,w=λj(1−α)y(ϕ)l(ϕ)  for each ϕ∈Uj with x(ϕ)>0p_j=\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}\lambda_j,\qquad w=\lambda_j(1-\alpha)\frac{y(\phi)}{l(\phi)}\ \text{ for each }\phi\in U_j\text{ with }x(\phi)>0pj​=ε−1ε​λj​,w=λj​(1−α)l(ϕ)y(ϕ)​  for each ϕ∈Uj​ with x(ϕ)>0

The payoff is the object used in the stability concept: a coalition has a dominating deviation if it can change contracts among its members so that no member's Πj\Pi_jΠj​ falls and at least one rises. Equation (12) later rewrites Πj\Pi_jΠj​ as profit on household sales plus net transfers of surplus.

The note writes the condition as an inequality because it is a constraint on the entrepreneur: at price pjp_jpj​ she cannot sell more than the household demands. With a positive marginal cost she never wants to sell less at a given price, so the constraint binds in equilibrium.

This is the technological (resource) constraint for good jjj. The left-hand side is the total use of the good: consumption cjc_jcj​ by the household plus the quantities x(ϕ)x(\phi)x(ϕ) shipped to each customer, where the sum runs over the downstream techniques DjD_jDj​. The right-hand side is total production of the good, the sum over the upstream techniques UjU_jUj​ of the output of each technique from equation (2), with input x(ϕ)x(\phi)x(ϕ) bought from the supplier s(ϕ)s(\phi)s(ϕ) and labor l(ϕ)l(\phi)l(ϕ).

Two features should be noted. First, the entrepreneur may in principle produce with several techniques at once, and the outputs are perfect substitutes because they are the same good. In equilibrium she uses only the technique that delivers the lowest marginal cost, equation (8), since each technique has constant returns. Second, the same x(ϕ)x(\phi)x(ϕ) appears on the left-hand side of the constraint of the supplier and on the right-hand side of the constraint of the buyer; this is what links entrepreneurs into supply chains.

The multiplier on this constraint in the problem of equation (3) is λj\lambda_jλj​, the marginal cost of good jjj, and efficiency is defined from it as qj≡w/λjq_j\equiv w/\lambda_jqj​≡w/λj​. The constraint, together with the labor resource constraint

∫01∑ϕ∈Ujl(ϕ)dj≤L\int_0^1\sum_{\phi\in U_j}l(\phi)dj\leq L∫01​ϕ∈Uj​∑​l(ϕ)dj≤L

defines resource feasibility. Resource feasibility alone is not enough in this model, because every good is produced with another good and chains are infinite: the constraint can be satisfied for every jjj by allocations in which inputs are borrowed from ever more distant upstream stages. This is why the note adds chain feasibility, equation (6). If UjU_jUj​ is empty, the right-hand side is zero and jjj cannot produce.

The condition is a definition, but the product on its right-hand side comes from combining the technologies along a chain. In the supply chain representation, stage nnn of chain ω\omegaω produces yn(ω)y^n(\omega)yn(ω) with the technology of equation (2), with y0(ω)=c(ω)y^0(\omega)=c(\omega)y0(ω)=c(ω) and xn(ω)=yn+1(ω)x^n(\omega)=y^{n+1}(\omega)xn(ω)=yn+1(ω). The recursion says that the entrepreneur selects the technique with the lowest unit cost, where the input is valued at the marginal cost of the supplier and not at a marked-up price. It does not determine efficiencies uniquely: qj=0q_j=0qj​=0 for all jjj is always a solution, which is the pairwise stable equilibrium without production, and solutions with infinite efficiency exist as well. Countable stability and chain feasibility select the solution in equation (9).

Consider a technique ϕ\phiϕ with buyer bbb and supplier sss. The pair can change its own contract, so pairwise stability requires that its terms maximize the joint payoff of the two, with all other contracts fixed.

Step 1, value of the input to the buyer. With multiplier λb\lambda_bλb​ on her constraint in equation (5), one more unit of the input is worth λb∂y∂x=λbαy(ϕ)x(ϕ)\lambda_b\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=\lambda_b\alpha\frac{y(\phi)}{x(\phi)}λb​∂x∂y​=λb​αx(ϕ)y(ϕ)​ to the buyer. is obtained by the same steps if the tax lowers the efficiency delivered by a technique one for one, that is, if it acts like dividing the productivity zzz of techniques with suppliers in group kkk by δk\delta_kδk​; then the intensity above is μkδk−ζθ0q−ζ\mu_k\delta_k^{-\zeta}\theta_0q^{-\zeta}μk​δk−ζ​θ0​q−ζ. This is the direct analogue of the trade share in Eaton and Kortum (2002), where the whole unit cost of a source is scaled by the trade cost. The note transcribes the paper correctly, but the result depends on how the tax enters, and the supplement should be consulted before the elasticity −ζ-\zeta−ζ is used for identification.
